name: Telegraph cryptic crossword, All New book 4 No 60

book.title: The Telegraph All New Cryptic Crosswords 4

blocks.note: la is the feminine French for 'the'
under a figure means less than it

explanation.surface: A sniffy remark that the French are not entirely spotless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'less than clean' reads as one phrase meaning grubby, but the last word stands alone as the definition, a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To launder is to wash and iron clothes or linen, so it means to clean them.

indicators.note: in a down clue, one thing on another sits below it, so the drug letter goes after the floor covering

blocks.note: a mat is a small carpet or rug
E is slang for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: A wild scene of rapture on the rug, explained away as being for a spouse.
explanation.definitionFit: Mate is an informal word for a spouse or partner, so it can stand for a husband.

indicators.note: being in a word means these letters go inside it

blocks.note: a rest is a break from work
one is I, and 's is short for is, so one's becomes I + S

explanation.surface: A soldier takes a pause from fighting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One's' reads as a possessive, but it is 'one is' contracted, I and S.
explanation.definitionFit: To resist is to fight against or oppose, so it means to combat something.

indicators.note: to change something is to alter its form, so these letters are put in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A strict person who has learned to change their ways and go easier.
explanation.definitionFit: A tolerant person puts up with faults, so they are forgiving and lenient in judgement.

blocks.note: a disco is a nightclub
M is the abbreviation for male
a bastion is a fortification, a fort

explanation.surface: A men-only club annoys those kept out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Club, male bastion' reads like a gentlemen's club; it splits into a dance venue, a gender abbreviation and a stronghold.
explanation.definitionFit: Discomfort is mild physical pain or unease, as from a rash, which matches irritation.

blocks.note: a con is a convict
form is British slang for a criminal record

explanation.surface: Police tailing an ex-prisoner who has previous convictions.
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang a criminal 'has form', meaning previous convictions.
explanation.definitionFit: To conform is to follow rules or custom, as in following the crowd.

blocks.note: rhyming slang: china plate = mate, so china means a pal
to aver is to state firmly

explanation.surface: A Chinese official travelling abroad on government affairs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'China' looks like the country; in Cockney rhyming slang a 'china plate' is a mate. In an across clue, A on B puts A after B, so the friend comes first.
explanation.definitionFit: Palaver is a fuss or carry-on, as in 'what's all this business?', an informal synonym.

indicators.note: one thing sitting in another means it is placed inside that other word

blocks.note: a moor is open heathland
a nit is a louse egg or young louse

explanation.surface: A naturalist told to watch for a bug out on the heath.
explanation.walkthrough: Heath could suggest the heather plant or Ted Heath; here it is open moorland with a tiny creature placed in the middle.
explanation.definitionFit: To monitor something is to keep watching it closely, a synonym for observing it.

indicators.note: perhaps hints that the letters may be arranged some other way

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A salon worker who lets others use the hood dryer.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a salon, which is where the answer works, so the letters are easy to miss as fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A hairdresser cuts and styles hair, and is often called a stylist in salons.

clue.text: The French turns in show? Saucy!

indicators.note: turning round means the French article is read from its end back to its start
sitting in the other word means these letters go inside it

blocks.note: le is French for 'the'
to indicate is to show or point out

explanation.surface: A French performer twirling in a risqué cabaret number.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turns' suggests a stage act, but it flips LE to EL, which goes into INDICATE: IND(EL)ICATE.
explanation.definitionFit: Something indelicate is slightly improper or risqué, just as a saucy joke is mildly rude.

indicators.note: in an across clue, one thing placed on another is written after it, so the doubled force follows the metal

blocks.note: Cu is the chemical symbol for copper
F stands for force; doubled it is two of them

explanation.surface: A police officer's patrol route reinforced with twice the manpower.
explanation.walkthrough: 'copper's beat' reads as a policeman's patrol, but copper is the metal Cu and beat is a verb. In an across clue, A on B puts A after B.
explanation.definitionFit: To cuff someone is to strike them with the open hand, so it means to beat or hit.

clue.text: One with a will of his own?

definitions.text: One with a will of his own?

blocks.clueFragment: One with a will of his own?
blocks.note: surface reading: a stubborn, independent-minded person who does as he pleases
setter's reading: someone who has drawn up his own legal will

explanation.walkthrough: 'A will of his own' is an idiom for headstrong; the question mark flags that a legal document is meant instead.
explanation.definitionFit: A testator is the legal term for a person who has made a will disposing of their estate.

indicators.note: something off is out of order or wrong, so the letters are set in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A golfer told the following tee is further away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'farther off' looks like one phrase about distance; the last word alone is the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Thereafter means after that, so it works as an adverb meaning next in time.

clue.text: Plug hole put on a pedestal

blocks.note: a plug is a piece of publicity, an ad
being in a hole is being in difficulties, in the mire

explanation.surface: A DIY job: stopping up a hole and then mounting something on a stand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plug' and 'hole' look like plumbing; here a plug is an advertisement and a hole is a fix you are stuck in.
explanation.definitionFit: To put someone on a pedestal is to idealise them, to hold them in high regard and esteem.

indicators.note: something broken has its parts scattered, so the letters are put back in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A request to fix two kitchen appliances that have stopped working.
explanation.definitionFit: Restoration is the work of returning something damaged to good condition, a noun synonym for repair.

indicators.note: made of these words means the letters are taken from inside the run of text

blocks.note: the letters run across the three words, dropping the start and the end
surface padding: it only finishes the picture of a cut crystal

explanation.surface: A cut gemstone with many facets worn as a lucky amulet.
explanation.definitionFit: A talisman is an object believed to bring luck or ward off evil, a lucky charm.

blocks.note: a flower bed is a garden plot
evil means wicked, cruel

explanation.surface: A villain hatching a scheme of cruel suffering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plot' reads as a scheme, but it is a patch of garden; the definition is the verb at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: To bedevil is to plague or harass persistently, so it means to torment.

blocks.note: war is armed battle
to rant is to shout or cry out angrily

explanation.surface: A rousing shout before a fight that lifts the troops.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Battle cry' reads as one thing, a war whoop, but the words split into two separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A warrant is a justification or authority, the grounds that support an action or claim.

clue.text: Happened to call around five, not four!

indicators.note: 'not four' says the numeral for four is taken away from the word before it
going around something means wrapping these letters about it

blocks.note: to give someone a bell is British slang for phoning them
the number word, taken as written
IV is four in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: Someone dropped in at five rather than four, as it turned out.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a visit timed for a different hour; 'five, not four' is the spelt-out number with the Roman numeral for four removed.
explanation.definitionFit: Befell is the past tense of befall, an old-fashioned verb meaning to happen or occur.

indicators.note: without its nucleus means the central letter of the word is removed
unstable things do not hold their arrangement, so the letters are reordered

blocks.note: taken as written; its middle letter is the fifth of nine

explanation.surface: A physics lab where short-lived particles decay away to nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unstable' and 'nucleus' read as nuclear physics; nucleus is the middle letter, I, which goes before the rest is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Spectral means ghostly, of or like a spectre, so it describes a phantom as an adjective.

blocks.note: an ex is a former partner
a tort is a civil wrong in law

explanation.surface: An ex-wife does wrong by threatening to reveal secrets.
explanation.walkthrough: A tort is the legal name for a civil wrong, such as negligence or trespass.
explanation.definitionFit: To extort is to obtain money by threats or force, which is what blackmail does.

blocks.note: first meaning: a complaint, a gripe
second meaning: the flesh of cattle

explanation.walkthrough: Grouse looks like the game bird, which would itself be meat; here it is the verb or noun for complaining.
explanation.definitionFit: Beef is slang for a grievance, as in 'what's your beef?', and also the meat from cows.

clue.text: Second little slut embracing the man's beloved

indicators.note: to embrace is to hold in the arms, so one word wraps round the other

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for second
wee is Scottish for small
tart is a slang term for a promiscuous woman
the pronoun for a man

explanation.surface: Gossip about a man's girlfriend being cheap.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's after 'the man' stands for 'is', joining the wordplay to the definition: S + WEE + T(HE)ART.
explanation.definitionFit: A sweetheart is a person one loves, a noun synonym for one's beloved.

indicators.note: being in a word means the letter is placed inside it

blocks.note: ego is a sense of self-importance
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A smug person who is so sure of being correct.
explanation.walkthrough: 'So' looks like an intensifier for right; it is the definition, the Latin for therefore.
explanation.definitionFit: Ergo is Latin for therefore, used in English to mean so or consequently.

indicators.note: a translation renders text into another form, so these letters are rendered in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A claim that converting books into Braille costs nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Liberal means generous or unrestricted, as in a liberal helping, close to free in sense.

clue.text: Criminal US soldier returns in disgrace

indicators.note: returning means going back, so the soldier is read from end to start
being in something means these letters are put inside that word

blocks.note: GI is the standard name for an American soldier
a brand is a mark of disgrace, a stigma

explanation.surface: An American serviceman comes home in shame after breaking the law.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Criminal' looks like an adjective for the soldier, but it is the definition, a noun here.
explanation.definitionFit: A brigand is a bandit or outlaw, especially one of a gang robbing travellers, so a criminal.
